01 · Overview

One record set, three ways to work it

This module is a working example built for the E-04 interaction-design brief. It shows that List, Card, and Kanban are three views of the same pipeline, not three separate features.

Search, filters, sort order, the status tab, and the current selection all live in one shared store. Switching between List, Card, and Kanban only changes how records are displayed. It never resets filters, clears the selection, or reloads data. The view, tab, filters, and sort are also saved in the URL, so a page refresh or a shared link returns to the same working set.

Day 1 · Module brief

Why CRM Opportunities

The brief suggested two candidates: HRMS Recruitment and CRM Opportunities. Opportunities was chosen because a sales pipeline is used in three different ways depending on the task, not because the table simply needed a redesign.

FieldNotes
Opportunity, Account, ContactText fields that identify the deal, the company, and the main contact there.
StageSeven fixed stages: Prospecting → Qualification → Needs Analysis → Proposal / Quote Sent → Negotiation → Closed – Won / Closed – Lost.
PriorityHigh / Medium / Low.
Value, ProbabilityA dollar amount and a 0–100% probability. Probability defaults by stage, from 10% at Prospecting to 100% at Closed-Won.
Close date, Last activityThe target or actual close date, and the date of the most recent activity.
Owner, SourceThe sales rep, and where the lead came from: referral, inbound, outbound, or partner.
Next step, Lost reasonFree text. Lost reason is recorded only when a deal is marked Closed-Lost.

The mock data has 50 records, spread unevenly across the pipeline on purpose: 13 at Prospecting, down to 5 at Negotiation, 4 Won, and 3 Lost. An even spread would have made every view equally easy to design for, which defeats the purpose of comparing them.

Why three views: the same 50 records answer three different questions. Qualifying and bulk-editing leads is a List task. Getting a feel for an account before a call is a Card task. Moving a deal from Negotiation to Closed-Won is a Kanban task. These are not one screen redrawn three times — each is built for a different kind of work.

02 · Architecture

Shared state, three renderers

One Zustand store holds the record set and every working value. List, Card, and Kanban all read from it through the same selector. None of them keeps its own copy of the data.

view · status · owner · priority · sort · dir — synced to the URL query string on every change

Day 2 · Framework rules

What a view switch is allowed to touch

The rule is simple: switching between List, Card, and Kanban changes only the presentation. Anything that defines which records are shown stays the same.

Carries across every switch

  • Search text
  • Owner filter, Priority filter
  • Status tab — All / Open / Won / Lost
  • Sort field and direction, including a manual drag-order
  • Selection — tracked by record id, not row position
  • An open detail drawer

Kept per view, not shared

  • Scroll position within that view
  • How much of the list is currently loaded — List renders all matching records at once; Card and Kanban each lazy-load their own batch

One exception: the brief asks for pagination to persist across a switch, the same as filters and sort. Right now, Card and Kanban reset to their first batch when you navigate away and back. Sort, filters, search, and selection all work correctly — this gap is called out rather than hidden.

03 · Presentation

The three views

Each view supports a different way of working the pipeline: dense comparison, visual scanning, or moving deals stage by stage. All three share the same record card, row-action menu, and stage-change rules.

01 List

Dense table for comparing and bulk-editing records.

  • Sortable columns with aria-sort
  • Inline-editable priority, owner, probability, close date
  • Drag handle for manual row reordering
  • Row click opens the detail drawer

02 Card

Responsive grid for visually browsing records.

  • Same card anatomy Kanban reuses, in its full form
  • Hover lift, drag-to-reorder grip
  • Loads in batches of 20 via IntersectionObserver

03 Kanban

Stage columns for pipeline movement.

  • Drag between stages, validated before it writes back
  • Column count + pipeline value, live
  • Each lane loads its own next batch independently
In the app

What it actually looks like

Real screenshots of the running prototype, not mockups. Same 50 records, same shared store, three views.

Internationalization

One layout, two directions

The language toggle switches the whole interface between English and Arabic. This is not a translated label on an English layout; the layout itself mirrors. Toggling it flips <html dir> between ltr and rtl, and every component built with Tailwind's logical-direction utilities (ps-/pe-, ms-/me-, start-/end- instead of fixed left/right) repositions itself automatically. There is no separate RTL stylesheet and no per-component "if Arabic" logic.

List — English (LTR)
List — العربية (RTL)

Column order, sort-arrow icons, the drag handle, and pagination controls all mirror. This is not the English table with the text flipped.

Kanban — English (LTR)
Kanban — العربية (RTL)

The stage columns reverse order too. Prospecting sits at the far right in Arabic, so the pipeline still reads start-to-end in the language's natural direction.

  • Every label, column header, empty state, and toast is fully translated, not machine-translated on the fly.
  • The sidebar, drawer position, sort icons, and drag handles all move to the opposite side, instead of staying pinned to the left.
  • Kanban's stage columns render in reverse order in Arabic, so the pipeline still reads start-to-end.
  • Currency and dates use Intl.NumberFormat and Intl.DateTimeFormat with the ar-AE locale. This locale uses Western numerals and a narrow currency symbol, matching how Gulf-region business software formats money.
  • Switching language never resets search, filters, sort, selection, or the current view. It follows the same rule as switching between List, Card, and Kanban: presentation only.
Day 2 · Competitor comparison

How six CRMs handle the same three views

Six CRMs, compared on how they switch views, and on what matters more: what happens to filters and selection when they do.

ProductView switcherKanbanCard / TileState preservation
Dynamics 365 Saved "Views" from a dropdown — List and Kanban are usually separate views, not one toggle. Tied to the business-process flow; a drag can require fields first. Not a real view type. Weak — each view is its own saved query, so filters often reset.
Oracle Sales List-first, with summary panels above the list. Only in service contexts; not part of core sales. Rarely used. Filters persist within one list, not across view types.
SAP Sales Cloud A toggle between List and a board. Strong rule enforcement — blocks a move until required fields are filled. Same as Kanban, not a separate view. Filters usually hold between List and Kanban.
Zoho CRM Live toggle — List / Kanban / Canvas. Group by any field, column totals, drag updates the field, bulk actions per column. "Canvas" is a real tile view, closer to Card than most. Strong — filters carry over between views.
Odoo Icon row — List / Kanban / Calendar / Graph / Pivot — everywhere. Its best view: grouped by stage, drag updates the field, columns show totals, quick-add per group. The Kanban card doubles as the tile. Excellent — nothing resets across views.
ClickUp Tab bar — List / Board / Table / Calendar / Gantt — saved per user. Fast drag, card previews, a custom cover field. A real gallery view, separate from Board. One of the strongest — filters and sort persist everywhere.

The pattern worth naming: Odoo, ClickUp, and Zoho keep state best because their views are just toggle buttons on one screen. Dynamics and Oracle keep it worst because each view is its own separately configured screen. That's the deciding factor — not how polished any single view looks.

Best answer — List

Table density and inline edit, like Dynamics and Oracle — but with Odoo and ClickUp's state persistence instead.

Built: sortable columns, inline-editable Priority / Owner / Probability / Close date, reading from the same filtered set as Card and Kanban.

Best answer — Card

Only Zoho and ClickUp treat Card as its own view, not Kanban without columns. Here, Card is for browsing, not tracking movement.

Built: the same card as Kanban, in full — including the stage badge Kanban hides — with no workflow grouping.

Best answer — Kanban

Odoo's direct-field drag, Zoho's totals and bulk actions, SAP/Dynamics' rule checks — plus what none of them do: explain a rejected move.

Built: every drop is validated first — no reopening closed deals, no skipping to Won, Lost needs a reason — with a visible reason when it's refused.
04 · Reference

Feature reference

Grouped by what each control does. Implemented means it works end-to-end against the in-memory data. Simulated stands in for a real backend call. Partial covers the common case, but not every edge case.

Search, filtering & sort

ControlBehavior
SearchMatches opportunity name, account, owner, and stage. Includes a 250ms debounce, a clear button, and a dedicated no-results state.Implemented
Owner / Priority filtersActive filters show as removable chips, plus a Clear all button. The filter model supports more fields without any restructuring.Implemented
Status tabsAll, Open, Won, and Lost. Open excludes both closed stages. Behavior is identical in all three views.Implemented
SortSort by name, account, value, probability, close date, owner, or stage (in pipeline order, not alphabetical). Column headers handle this in List; a dropdown handles it everywhere else.Implemented
Manual drag orderDragging a row or card sets sort to "Custom order," built from what's on screen at that moment.Implemented

Selection & bulk actions

ControlBehavior
SelectionTracked by record ID, not row position, so it survives switching between List, Card, and Kanban.Implemented
Bulk toolbarA floating bar at the bottom center: change owner, change priority, change stage, export selected, or delete.Implemented
Bulk stage changeRuns every record through the same checks as a single drag. If some fail, it shows "6 updated, 2 couldn't be" with a reviewable list.Implemented

Record actions & the drawer

ControlBehavior
Edit / Delete iconsShown directly on the row or card, not buried in a menu. Delete opens a confirmation dialog first.Implemented
"…" menuView, Duplicate, Move to (stage), Change owner, Change priority, and Export. The same menu is used in List, Card, and Kanban.Implemented
Detail drawerA slide-over panel for quick viewing and editing: stage, priority, probability, close date, and owner, all inline. Opening or closing it never affects search, filters, sort, or scroll position.Implemented
Create / Edit formOne validated dialog handles both. The "+" button on a Kanban column pre-fills that stage.Implemented
ExportExports a CSV of the current filtered set, or just the selection.Implemented

Drag, drop & business rules

RuleBehavior
Closed stays closedA Closed-Won or Closed-Lost record can't be reopened by dragging. Reopen it from the record itself.Implemented
No skipping to WonClosed-Won is only reachable from Negotiation.Implemented
Lost needs a reasonMoving to Closed-Lost requires a reason first, through a dialog, before the change is saved.Implemented
Permission checkA record the current user can't edit simply can't be picked up. It isn't rejected after the fact.Implemented
Keyboard alternative"Move to" in the "…" menu runs the same checks as dragging, for keyboard and touch users.Implemented
Optimistic rollbackA move applies right away, then is confirmed in the background. If confirmation fails, the record rolls back and a toast explains why.Simulated
05 · Design system

Tokens, not one-off values

Blue is reserved for primary actions, selected navigation, the selected view, focus, and selected table rows. Everywhere else, surfaces stay neutral. Status colors are separate from the accent color, and never carry meaning through color alone; every badge also has a text label.

Semantic colors use a darker, 700-equivalent shade rather than the more common 500–600 shade. This keeps badge text readable (at least 4.5:1 contrast) against its own pastel background, not just against white.

06 · Accessibility

Built to WCAG 2.2 AA

Built to meet WCAG 2.2 AA, and checked against contrast, keyboard navigation, and semantics, not just reviewed by eye.

  • Sortable List headers use aria-sort, verified to toggle correctly between none, ascending, and descending.
  • Icon-only controls have descriptive labels, such as "Edit — Northgate Manufacturing" instead of just "Edit."
  • Rows and cards work with a keyboard: Tab to focus, then Enter or Space to open the record.
  • Stage moves also work without dragging: "Move to" in the "…" menu runs the same checks.
  • Status is never shown by color alone; every badge also has a text label.
  • Focus is always visible, with a 2px ring on every interactive control, including table rows.
  • prefers-reduced-motion is respected across the whole app, not component by component.
  • Result counts and loading regions use aria-live and aria-busy so screen readers announce changes.
07 · Loading & performance

Skeletons that match, loading that doesn't block

Each view has its own loading skeleton, shaped like its real layout rather than a generic rectangle. It shows briefly on first load, then fades into the real content.

List skeleton

Table rows shaped like the real columns: checkbox, name, account, badges, value, date, owner.

Card skeleton

Card-shaped placeholders in the same grid, loading in batches of 20 as the user scrolls near the end.

Kanban skeleton

Column-shaped placeholders. Each lane loads its next batch on its own, independently of the others.

All entrance and hover animation uses only opacity and transform, never width, height, or position. Card fade-in is staggered for only the first 12 items, so a large batch never triggers a long cascade of animations.
